notes: Conspiracy to defraud unanimity appeal; Hancock/Brown/Landy analysis is detailed and authoritative.

enrichment.short_title: K, G & M: Brown direction and particulars in conspiracy to defraud
key_facts: After a 133-day trial the appellants were convicted of conspiracy to defraud shareholders of H plc by inducing investment in a hollow shell company that never acquired rights to product C.
The indictment listed twelve false representations (a)-(l) but the judge directed that unanimity on any particular representation was not required.
Each appellant appealed principally on whether the jury should have been directed to be unanimous on at least one specified representation.
G was sentenced to two years' imprisonment and M to a 200-hour community punishment order; K had not yet been sentenced.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal (Criminal Division) appeal by leave on a Brown/Mitchell unanimity direction in a long-running conspiracy to defraud trial.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the judge's direction was not a misdirection and the convictions were safe, though the court criticised the trial length and urged clearer indictment drafting separating agreement from overt acts.
enrichment.ratio: In conspiracy to defraud the essential ingredient is a sufficiently certain dishonest agreement to defraud; particulars under Landy inform the charge but are not ingredients requiring jury unanimity unless they define the agreement itself, following Hancock; Brown applies to ingredients, not to overt acts from which an agreement may be inferred.
legal_issues: Whether jury unanimity was required on at least one of the twelve specified false representations
Whether particulars in a conspiracy to defraud indictment become essential ingredients of the offence
How Hancock, Bennett and Brown apply to common-law conspiracy to defraud
Whether the trial judge misdirected the jury on the agreement alleged
linked_authorities: Brown (1984) 79 Cr App R 115
R v Hancock [1996] 2 Cr App R 554
R v Landy [1981] 1 WLR 355
Scott v Metropolitan Police [1975] AC 819

notes: Complex asbestos bankruptcy and pension scheme directions; trustee discretion analysis is thorough.

enrichment.short_title: T&N pension trustees: voting on Federal Mogul Chapter 11 plan
key_facts: Trustees of the T&N Retirement Benefits Scheme sought directions on whether to vote against Federal Mogul's US Chapter 11 reorganisation plan.
T&N's asbestos liabilities drove FMG into bankruptcy; the plan would swap asbestos claims for equity via an Asbestos Trust with a controversial 50.1/49.9 split with US noteholders.
The scheme had about 37,200 members and actuarial deficits ranging from £97m on an MFR basis to £917m on a buy-out basis.
Plan options included 'Let it Run' and alternative Class H dividends calculated by T&N Distribution Ratios that the trustees considered inadequate.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Chancery application for directions on how independent and employer trustees should exercise their discretion in voting on a published US bankruptcy plan.
enrichment.outcome: The court directed that the trustees were permitted not to accept or support the Plan; rejecting it in favour of pursuing recoveries through English administration was a reasonable exercise of trustee discretion.
enrichment.ratio: On a trustee direction application the court does not substitute its own commercial judgment but asks whether trustees have taken relevant matters into account and reached a conclusion a reasonable body of trustees could reach; Let it Run was unfair and a controlled realisation offered better recoveries than the Plan's dividends.
legal_issues: Whether trustees could permissibly vote against the Chapter 11 plan
Whether Let it Run or Alternative Treatment adequately protected scheme members
Whether statutory MFR and section 75 liabilities could be compromised in advance
How T&N Distribution Ratios undervalued trustee claims relative to controlled realisation
linked_authorities: Edge v Pensions Ombudsman [1998] Ch 512
Bradstock Group Pension Scheme Trustees Ltd v Bradstock Group Plc [2002] PLR 327
Forbes v Jackson [2004] EWHC 2361 (Ch)

confidence.notes: Directions on voting are clear; second issue on OPRA referral was deferred pending revised plan proposals.

notes: Insurance preliminary issues on assumed facts; causation and exclusion construction are clearly resolved.

enrichment.short_title: Tektrol v Hanover: virus and burglary exclusions in all-risks policy
key_facts: Tektrol sought business interruption cover under a Combined All Risks Policy after total loss of its industrial motor control source code.
A Christmas-card email virus deliberately erased copies on a laptop and remote backup; a burglary two weeks later stole remaining computers and the sole hard copy.
The trial was limited to two preliminary issues on agreed assumed facts under exclusions 7(b)(i) and 7(b)(ii).
Insurers argued either excluded cause was sufficient to defeat the entire claim because no copy survived.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Commercial Court trial of preliminary issues on assumed facts concerning business interruption exclusions in a property/all-risks policy.
enrichment.outcome: Both preliminary issues answered in the affirmative; consequential loss was excluded under exclusion 7(b)(i) for deliberate erasure by malicious persons and under 7(b)(ii) because the burglary loss did not result from a Defined Peril.
enrichment.ratio: Exclusion 7's 'directly or indirectly' language captures both the virus and burglary as causes of the business interruption; where one excluded cause suffices the claim fails, and 'loss' in exclusion 7(b)(ii) includes physical loss of records and software not merely electronic erasure.
legal_issues: Whether the virus erasure was 'caused deliberately' by malicious persons within exclusion 7(b)(i)
Whether burglary theft of computers fell within exclusion 7(b)(ii) or exclusion 13
Whether either excluded cause was enough to exclude the entire claim
Construction of 'Defined Peril' and 'malicious persons'
linked_authorities: Wayne Tank and Pump v Employers Liability Ltd [1974] 1 QB 57
Coxe v Employers' Liability Assurance Corporation Ltd [1916] 2 KB 629
Spinney's v Royal Insurance Co Ltd [1980] 1 Lloyd's Rep 406

notes: Short interlocutory strike injunction judgment; trade dispute analysis under s.221 is clear.

enrichment.short_title: LSC v PCS: strike injunction refused for NDPB trade dispute

statutes_considered.title: Trade Union and Labour Relations (Consolidation) Act 1992

key_facts: The Public and Commercial Services Union called out about 1,734 of 4,000 Learning and Skills Council staff on a one-day strike.
The dispute followed the Chancellor's July 2004 spending review and Gershon efficiency targets affecting NDPBs and public sector pay.
PCS sought six guarantees from LSC mirroring demands made of the Civil Service; LSC replied there were no current proposals for job cuts or transfers.
LSC contended there was no trade dispute and that the strike would not be in contemplation or furtherance of one.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Queen's Bench interlocutory application for an injunction to restrain imminent industrial action under section 221 of the 1992 Act.
enrichment.outcome: Injunction refused; a genuine trade dispute existed and the union was more likely than not to establish a section 219 defence at trial.
enrichment.ratio: Whether a trade dispute exists is an objective question but may draw on the parties' states of mind; assurances that there are 'no proposals' do not necessarily extinguish a dispute where broader public-sector reform announcements raise legitimate concerns for NDPB employees.
legal_issues: Whether a trade dispute existed between LSC and PCS within section 244
Whether proposed strike action was in contemplation or furtherance of a trade dispute
Application of the section 221 likelihood-of-success test for interlocutory relief
Whether correspondence mirroring Civil Service guarantees showed a sham dispute
linked_authorities: Conway v Wade (1909) AC 522

confidence.notes: Interlocutory refusal is clearly reasoned; merits of the underlying dispute were not decided.

notes: Long investment negligence trial; advisory-account analysis and causation findings are comprehensive.

enrichment.short_title: Valse Holdings v Merrill Lynch: negligent investment advice claim dismissed
key_facts: Valse Holdings, a Panama company owned by the Djafar Mohseni Family Trust, claimed about US$3.93m loss from Merrill Lynch's advisory management of a concentrated technology-heavy portfolio from 1999 to 2002.
Mohammed Mohseni gave day-to-day instructions; the account was advisory not discretionary and leveraged through a US$10m credit facility.
Contractual terms designated Mohseni an expert investor to whom suitability protections did not apply.
Portfolio value fell sharply after the March 2000 Nasdaq peak despite repeated written diversification advice.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Commercial Court trial of claim for negligent investment advice, portfolio suitability and unauthorised trading on an advisory private client account.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; no breach of duty as to portfolio suitability and even if there had been breach it was not causative because Mohseni knowingly pursued his chosen high-risk strategy.
enrichment.ratio: On an advisory account where the client is contractually treated as an expert investor, the bank is not liable for failing to impose a diversified benchmark strategy the client repeatedly rejected; a knowing informed investor who disregards advice cannot recover losses caused by market downturn and his own instructions.
legal_issues: Whether Merrill Lynch owed a duty to advise on overall portfolio suitability against stated investment objectives
Effect of expert-investor contractual exclusions on FSA suitability rules
Whether unauthorised trading allegations succeeded
Causation and measure of damages on an incremental basis

confidence.notes: Final dismissal and causation analysis are explicit; detailed fact findings on Mohseni's control of trading.

notes: Wrongful birth liability trial; extensive expert evidence on fetal ultrasound and Bolam applied.

enrichment.short_title: Lillywhite v UCLH: holoprosencephaly scan negligence claim fails
key_facts: Alice Lillywhite was born with severe semilobar holoprosencephaly after Professor Rodeck reported a normal fetal brain scan at about 18 weeks in December 1991.
Sonographer Mrs Wright had earlier failed to visualise the cavum septum pellucidum and referred to a tertiary centre; Dr Meire and Dr Haeusler also reported normality.
Parents claimed damages for their own loss arising from the birth of a severely disabled child they would have terminated if properly diagnosed.
The case was tried nearly 15 years after the events with no scan images preserved from the tertiary examinations.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Queen's Bench liability trial on whether the 1991 ultrasound scan was negligent and whether termination would have been chosen.
enrichment.outcome: Negligence not established on the balance of probabilities; claim failed though the judge found without hesitation that the parents would have terminated had holoprosencephaly been diagnosed.
enrichment.ratio: Where three experienced tertiary sonologists were convinced by mimicking echoes and a careful scan showed no associated abnormalities, failure to diagnose semilobar holoprosencephaly at 18 weeks in 1991 did not fall below the ordinary skill of the specialty; Penney v East Kent/Bolitho principles require a logically defensible expert view.
legal_issues: Whether Professor Rodeck's scan fell below the standard of a tertiary fetal medicine consultant in 1991
What structures could have produced mimicking echoes for cavum septum, anterior horns and falx
Whether semilobar holoprosencephaly should routinely have been detectable at 18-20 weeks
Whether parents would have accepted termination if offered
linked_authorities: Penney, Palmer and Cannon v East Kent Health Authority [2000] PNLR 323
Bolitho v City and Hackney Health Authority [1998] AC 232
Maynard v West Midlands Regional Health Authority [1984] 1 WLR 634

confidence.notes: Detailed liability findings and termination counterfactual are clearly recorded.

notes: CPR 19.5 substitution after limitation; Horne-Roberts and Parsons applied with full CPR context.

enrichment.short_title: Kesslar v Moore & Tibbits: CPR 19.5 substitution after limitation expiry
key_facts: Miss Kesslar sued Moore & Tibbits (incorporating Kundert & Co) for conveyancing negligence by Andrea Roughley in 1997, but Roughley and Kundert were the actual partners of the predecessor firm.
Proceedings were issued against the successor firm on 21 August 2003, one day before limitation expired; defendants denied they were the correct party on 4 September.
Claimant applied under CPR 19.5(3)(a) to substitute Kundert and Roughley after limitation had passed.
Defendants had corresponded for months without asserting they were the wrong firm.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal on permission to substitute correct defendant solicitors after expiry of limitation under CPR 19.5 and section 35 of the Limitation Act 1980.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; substitution of Kundert and Roughley ordered as the claim form named Moore & Tibbits in mistake for the intended defendants.
enrichment.ratio: CPR 19.5(3)(a) is not confined to strict misnomer but applies where the claimant always intended to sue a person identifiable by a case-specific description but mistakenly named another; a mistake as to how to implead the intended tortfeasor falls within Horne-Roberts and Parsons v George.
legal_issues: Whether naming the successor firm was a mistake for the original partners within CPR 19.5(3)(a)
Distinction between mistake of identity/name and mistake as to legal liability or capacity
Application of Horne-Roberts v SmithKline Beecham and Parsons v George
Whether discretion should refuse substitution
linked_authorities: Horne-Roberts v SmithKline Beecham [2002] 1 WLR 1662
Parsons v George [2004] EWCA Civ 912
The Sardinia Sulcis [1991] 1 Lloyd's Rep 201

notes: Falun Gong asylum appeal; social group and imputed political opinion analysis carefully reasoned.

enrichment.short_title: L (China): Falun Gong refugee claim remitted on Convention grounds
key_facts: A Chinese Falun Gong practitioner sought asylum after two detentions and ill-treatment for distributing literature and organising practice sessions.
An adjudicator allowed her appeal on membership of a social group and Articles 2, 3 and 5 ECHR; the IAT overturned this on particular social group grounds.
Country evidence showed Falun Gong was banned in China from 1999 with widespread arbitrary arrest and ill-treatment of practitioners.
The appellant said she would continue Falun Gong activities if returned, but also told the IAT she was not wanted by police.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal on Immigration Appeal Tribunal decision refusing asylum; particular social group and internal flight issues raised by the tribunal of its own motion.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed and case remitted to a differently constituted IAT; membership of a particular social group was not made out but imputed political opinion may be the better Convention ground on the evidence.
enrichment.ratio: Falun Gong membership lacks the immutable characteristics required for a Refugee Convention particular social group under Shah and Montoya because adherence is voluntary and private practice is possible; authoritarian pressure to cease public practice does not require renunciation of core human rights entitlements, but imputed political opinion may suffice for active practitioners.
legal_issues: Whether Falun Gong practitioners constitute a particular social group under the Refugee Convention
Application of Shah, Montoya and Acosta immutable-characteristics test
Whether imputed political opinion is the appropriate Convention ground
Effect of appellant's evidence that she was not on a wanted list
linked_authorities: R v IAT ex p Shah [1999] 2 AC 629
Montoya [2002] EWCA Civ 620
A v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2002] EWCA Civ 1171

confidence.notes: Remittal rather than final grant; IAT did not accept all adjudicator fact findings.

notes: Multi-application commercial dispute; summary judgment and freezing order rulings are clearly listed.

enrichment.short_title: Trade Credit Finance v Bilgin: guarantee summary judgment and freezing order
key_facts: TCF sold a Goss printing press to Turkish publisher Sabah under a conditional sale agreement with retention of title; Dinc Bilgin guaranteed payment of the last six instalments.
Sabah defaulted on instalments 5-10 and TCF assigned the guarantee to NatWest; Bilgin's Isle of Man company Lime held Chelsea property transferred before the finance deal.
Claimants obtained a worldwide freezing order up to £4m; Lime sought summary judgment disputing TCF's title and beneficial ownership of the property.
Bilgin alleged fraud and improper police disclosure but failed to show criminal or illegal conduct in obtaining evidence.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Commercial Court hearing of six interlocutory applications including cross-applications for summary judgment, continuation/discharge of freezing injunction, and specific disclosure.
enrichment.outcome: Summary judgment for claimants against Bilgin on the guarantee; summary judgment for Lime against claimants; freezing order continued against Bilgin and his interest in Lime assets subject to modification for Mrs Bilgin; other applications failed or were adjourned.
enrichment.ratio: A personal guarantee of unpaid conditional-sale instalments warrants summary judgment where liability is undisputed; a freezing order may continue despite non-disclosure if the breach is not sufficiently serious, but should be limited to the judgment debtor's assets rather than a non-debtor spouse's interest.
legal_issues: Whether Bilgin's guarantee liability warranted summary judgment
Whether TCF retained title and could recover against Lime
Whether the freezing injunction should be discharged for material non-disclosure
Whether claimants improperly obtained police information in breach of the Data Protection Act 1984
linked_authorities: Miles v Bull [1969] 1 QB 258
Dubai Aluminium Co Ltd v Al Alawi [1999] 1 WLR 1964
Memory Corporation Plc v Sidhu (No 2) [2000] 1 WLR 1443

notes: Important jurisdiction conflict over Canadian s.46 and English exclusive forum clause; anti-suit reasoning is detailed.

enrichment.short_title: OT Africa Line v Magic: English jurisdiction clause and Canadian s.46
key_facts: OTAL sued cargo interests for a CAD 30,000 short-delivery claim on a bill of lading with an exclusive English law and High Court jurisdiction clause.
Canadian insurers subrogating Magic and Blue Banana commenced parallel proceedings in Toronto relying on section 46 of the Canadian Maritime Liability Act.
Gross J granted an anti-suit injunction against Magic and Blue Banana; Canadian courts upheld their jurisdiction and found Canada forum conveniens.
OTAL joined Canadian insurers alleging procuring breach of contract and sought extension of the anti-suit injunction.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Commercial Court applications on service out, stay, discharge or extension of anti-suit injunctions in parallel English and Canadian cargo short-delivery proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Insurers' challenge to service largely failed; stay and discharge applications refused; anti-suit injunction extended to insurers; English proceedings to continue under the exclusive jurisdiction clause despite Canadian section 46.
enrichment.ratio: Section 46 of the Canadian Maritime Liability Act does not create an exceptional circumstance justifying departure from ordinary principles enforcing exclusive jurisdiction clauses; parties should be held to their English forum agreement unless strong reasons exist, and insurers who control Canadian proceedings may be injuncted from breaching an existing anti-suit order.
legal_issues: Whether Canadian section 46 justified staying English proceedings or discharging the anti-suit injunction
Whether Canadian insurers could be served for procuring breach of contract under CPR 6.20(8)(a)
Whether a third-party costs order basis supported service under CPR 6.20(17)
Whether anti-suit relief should extend to non-party insurers
linked_authorities: Donohue v Armco [2002] 1 Lloyd's Rep 425
Turner v Grovit [2004] 2 Lloyd's Rep 169
Union Discount Co v Zoller [2002] 1 WLR 517
